items.title: UCCE Hosts Rice Production Workshop March 18-19
items.description: DAVIS, Calif. — Rice growers and other agricultural professionals across the Sacramento Valley are invited to attend the 2026 Rice Production Workshop, a two-day educational program focused on the principles and practices of rice production in California. The workshop will take place March 18–19, from 8:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. each day, at Lundberg Family […] The post UCCE Hosts Rice Production Workshop March 18-19 appeared first on Morning Ag Clips.
items.summary:
The UC Cooperative Extension (UCCE) is hosting a 2-day Rice Production Workshop on March 18-19, 2026 in Richvale, Butte County, California. The workshop will focus on the principles and practices of rice production in the state, with topics including rice growth and development, land formation, varieties, planting, water/fertility management, weed control, pests, and diseases.

The event is targeted at rice growers and agricultural professionals in the Sacramento Valley region. It will be presented by UCCE specialists and advisors, including Bruce Linquist, Whitney Brim-DeForest, Kassim Al-Khatib, Luis Espino, Michelle Leinfelder-Miles, Ian Grettenberger, and Sarah Marsh Janish.

The registration fee is $200, which includes a workshop manual and lunch both days. The registration deadline is March 15, 2026. Continuing education credits from the California Department of Pesticide Regulation and the California Certified Crop Adviser Program have been requested.

For more information or to register, contact the UCCE Sutter-Yuba Office at (530) 822-7515 or visit the event website at https://ucanr.edu/blog/sjc-and-delta-field-crops/article/meeting-announcement-rice-production-workshop.

items.title: The Expanding Role of Micronutrients in a Tight Margin Era
items.description: As margins tighten, micronutrients gain importance, helping growers and retailers protect yield, improve efficiency, and maximize returns amid economic uncertainty. The post The Expanding Role of Micronutrients in a Tight Margin Era appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
Micronutrients are becoming increasingly critical for farmers as profit margins shrink. They can help maintain yields, improve efficiency, and maximize returns during economic volatility. Key points:

- Micronutrient use has increased 15-20% in the past 5 years as growers seek ways to protect yields and improve efficiency.
- Prices for key micronutrients like zinc and boron have risen 40-50% in the past year due to supply chain issues and rising input costs.
- Farmers are using more targeted micronutrient applications, such as in-furrow or foliar sprays, to address specific deficiencies and maximize returns.
- Retailers are expanding micronutrient product offerings and education to help growers optimize micronutrient use for their specific crops and conditions.
- Experts recommend that farmers work closely with agronomists to develop a customized micronutrient program based on soil tests, crop needs, and economic conditions.
- Proper micronutrient management can boost yields by 5-10 bushels/acre for corn and 2-4 bushels/acre for soybeans, helping offset tight margins.

items.title: Biologicals and the Row Crop Conundrum
items.description: Biologicals are definitely gaining momentum across many parts of the agricultural world, but row crop usage remains an issue. The post Biologicals and the Row Crop Conundrum appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
While biologicals are gaining traction in other agricultural sectors, their usage in row crops remains limited.

Key statistics:
- Biologicals account for only 5-10% of the total crop protection market in the U.S.
- The global biologicals market is expected to grow from $8 billion in 2020 to $17 billion by 2025, a 16% annual growth rate.
- However, row crops account for only 25-30% of the total biologicals market.

Reasons for slow adoption in row crops:
- Inconsistent product performance compared to traditional chemical pesticides
- Lack of broad-spectrum activity and limited residual control
- Challenges in scaling production and distribution
- Higher costs compared to chemical alternatives

Impacts on farmers:
- Limited options for biological pest and disease control in row crops
- Potential missed opportunities to reduce chemical inputs and improve sustainability

Recommendations:
- Continued investment in R&D to improve biologicals' efficacy and reliability
- Collaboration between industry, universities, and government to address regulatory and scaling challenges
- Education and outreach to help farmers understand the benefits and proper use of biologicals

Quotes:
"We need to keep working to improve the consistency, efficacy, and economics of biologicals to drive greater adoption in row crops," said an industry expert.

items.title: How Connected Technology Is Protecting Grain Quality From Bin to Market
items.description: As grain storage expands, connected technologies are helping to reduce post-harvest losses through real-time monitoring, remote control, and data-driven insights. The post How Connected Technology Is Protecting Grain Quality From Bin to Market appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
As grain storage capacity has expanded, connected sensors and software are enabling farmers to better monitor grain quality and condition in storage bins. This allows them to make more informed decisions to prevent spoilage and maintain grain quality from bin to market. Key points:

- Connected technologies like sensors, controls, and software platforms are enabling real-time monitoring and remote management of grain storage bins.
- This helps farmers detect issues early, like temperature changes or moisture buildup, to prevent spoilage and maintain grain quality.
- Data analytics provide insights to optimize storage conditions and handling processes, reducing post-harvest losses.
- Examples include sensors that detect grain moisture, temperature, and carbon dioxide levels, connected to software platforms that alert farmers to potential problems.
- Technologies allow remote control of aeration fans, humidity, and other storage conditions to maintain ideal environments.
- Benefits include better preservation of grain quality, reduced spoilage and losses, and more informed decisions on when to sell grain.
- Experts note connected technologies are critical as grain storage capacity has expanded, helping farmers safeguard their harvests.

items.title: Subpar Snowpack Pushes Back Crop Plans for Farmers
items.description: SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Despite a strong start to California’s wet season, snowpack conditions remain below average. A deficient snowpack could mean less water available for summer irrigation, threatening to cut surface water deliveries to farmers. Rainfall at the end of last year helped boost water supplies, enough so that the U.S. Drought Monitor reported no […] The post Subpar Snowpack Pushes Back Crop Plans for Farmers appeared first on Morning Ag Clips.
items.summary:
Key points:

- California's snowpack is currently at 59% of average as of late January 2026, raising concerns about water availability for summer irrigation and potential impact on crop plans.

- The state saw a strong start to the wet season, but conditions dried up in January, with most precipitation coming as rain rather than snowpack.

- Recent storms have helped, but there is still uncertainty if the snowpack will reach average levels by the typical peak in April.

- Snowpack provides about 30% of California's water supply, with agriculture accounting for 40% of the state's total water use and 80% of water used by homes and businesses.

- Farmers like Aaron Barcellos and Brian Medeiros are already adjusting their crop plans, likely reducing water-intensive crops like cotton in favor of more drought-tolerant permanent crops like almonds, olives, and pomegranates.

- The variability in weather patterns, with oscillation between wet and dry periods, is making crop planning difficult for farmers this year.

- Experts like Jay Lund from UC Davis say it's hard to predict the final snowpack levels until the end of March, as California has seen both very dry and very wet years.

items.title: FarmPath Seeks 300 New and Aspiring Farmers for Free, National Program
items.description: LIBERTYVILLE, Ill. — Applications are now open for FarmPath, a national, multi-year program designed to make farming more accessible and achievable for aspiring and beginning farmers across the United States. The program is supported by The Mosaic Company Foundation for Sustainable Food Systems and The PepsiCo Foundation whose investments reflect a shared focus on helping […] The post FarmPath Seeks 300 New and Aspiring Farmers for Free, National Program appeared first on Morning Ag Clips.
items.summary:
The FarmPath program is a national, multi-year program designed to make farming more accessible and achievable for aspiring and beginning farmers across the United States. The program is supported by The Mosaic Company Foundation for Sustainable Food Systems and The PepsiCo Foundation, with a shared focus on helping to strengthen the next generation of farmers and build a more resilient food system.

The program provides practical education in best practices for resilient agriculture and farm management, access to experienced mentors, and connection to a national network of professionals working across food and agriculture. It integrates training in production skills with in-depth instruction on the systems, markets, and decisions that shape long-term success. The program also offers up to $10,000 in implementation funding for participants.

FarmPath is open to a wide range of participants, including farm-raised innovators, urban and community growers, career changers, and early-stage farmers seeking to diversify or strengthen their operations. Applications are open through March 23, 2026, and up to 300 participants will be selected for Year One, with competitive progression into Years Two and Three.

The program is a collaboration between the Farm Foundation, a 501(c)(3) non-profit accelerator of practical solutions for agriculture, and the Mosaic Company Foundation for Sustainable Food Systems, as well as the PepsiCo Foundation, the philanthropic arm of PepsiCo.

items.title: Cultivating Tomorrow: Breeding’s Hidden Constraint: Why Execution, Not Data, Will Define AgTech Winners
items.description: Meiogenix CEO Ricardo Garcia de Alba argues execution — not prediction — will unlock stalled traits and define AgTech winners in 2026. The post Cultivating Tomorrow: Breeding’s Hidden Constraint: Why Execution, Not Data, Will Define AgTech Winners appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
Meiogenix CEO Ricardo Garcia de Alba states that execution, not data, will be the key factor defining winners in AgTech by 2026. He argues that while data collection and prediction models have advanced, the bottleneck is in executing and implementing improved traits. 

Only 5% of AgTech startups are focused on execution, while 95% are focused on data and prediction. However, the real challenge is translating data into scaled field performance. For example, while AI can predict which traits will improve crop yields, the key is actually getting those traits into commercial varieties.

Garcia de Alba believes the winners in AgTech by 2026 will be companies that prioritize execution and delivering improved traits to farmers. He argues that in the next 5 years, the industry needs to shift focus from data collection to trait implementation. This will require new processes, partnerships, and investment in execution capabilities.

Overall, the article emphasizes that the future of AgTech will be defined by the ability to transform data insights into real-world agricultural improvements, rather than data analytics alone. Farmers need tangible results, not just predictive models.

items.title: In Oregon, a Local Seafood Movement Connects Consumers to the Coast
items.description: “The fishing industry has taken a lot of hits in the last few years, and most of them hit the small guys the hardest,” says Dixon. “We’re seeing more and more families not being able to afford to maintain a small commercial fishing vessel, leading to more large businesses taking over.” Dixon, a co-founder of […] The post In Oregon, a Local Seafood Movement Connects Consumers to the Coast appeared first on Civil Eats.
items.summary:
The fishing industry in Oregon has faced significant challenges in recent years, with small-scale commercial fishermen struggling to maintain their businesses. As larger companies take over, many families are unable to afford to maintain small commercial fishing vessels.

To address this issue, a local seafood movement has emerged, led by organizations such as Catch It Coastal and the Cannon Beach Farmers Market. These initiatives work to promote locally-caught seafood and provide direct-to-consumer sales opportunities for small-scale fishermen.

The Cannon Beach Farmers Market, for example, has seen a significant increase in seafood sales, with 25% of total sales coming from seafood in 2021, up from 10% in previous years. This has provided a crucial outlet for local fishermen to sell their catch and connect with consumers.

The article highlights the story of fisherman Brock Dixon, who has benefited from the local seafood movement. Dixon says the movement has helped his business, allowing him to maintain his small commercial fishing vessel and continue providing high-quality seafood to local consumers.

Overall, the local seafood movement in Oregon is playing a vital role in supporting small-scale commercial fishermen and providing consumers with access to fresh, locally-sourced seafood. This trend has the potential to strengthen coastal communities and promote sustainable fishing practices.

items.title: High demand dwindles hay supplies as dry weather persists
items.description: Texas Crop and Weather Report - Feb. 24, 2026 The post High demand dwindles hay supplies as dry weather persists appeared first on AgriLife Today.
items.summary:
A bumper hay crop in 2025 initially provided a surplus, but that supply is now dwindling as livestock producers rely on it amid the ongoing dry weather.

- Hay supplies are tightening in drier areas, while other regions remain well-stocked. Round bale prices range from $75-$85 on average, with premium bales $110-$145.
- Rainfall deficits of 8 inches or more since September have severely impacted grazing and pasture recovery across central and west Texas. Some areas have received small amounts of rain, but more substantial precipitation is needed.
- The pasture mealybug, an invasive pest, is raising concerns among hay producers in South Texas if it continues to spread.
- The long-range forecast calls for above-normal temperatures and below-normal rainfall, further straining hay and grazing outlook.
- Livestock producers are heavily supplementing cattle diets with hay and feed as pasture conditions remain poor. Some have started shipping animals.
- Winter wheat is in poor to fair condition overall, with varying impacts from the dry weather depending on location. Warm-season forage production is also expected to be low.
- Texas A&M AgriLife Extension experts say a major rainfall event is needed across the state to help replenish soil moisture, pastures, and improve prospects for the upcoming growing season.

items.summary: The EPA has repealed a 2024 rule that placed stricter limits on mercury emissions from coal-fired power plants, the primary source of mercury that accumulates in fish. Experts warn that this decision could have significant negative impacts on agricultural communities and encourage the EPA to reconsider its position and reinstate the regulations to protect public health and the environment.

items.title: New Mexico dairy named in Fairlife animal-welfare lawsuit
items.description: A lawsuit alleging animal mistreatment at a New Mexico dairy has raised new questions about Fairlife’s supply chain and animal welfare claims. The post New Mexico dairy named in Fairlife animal-welfare lawsuit appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
A federal lawsuit alleges animal mistreatment at Woodcrest Dairy near Roswell, New Mexico, and that milk from this dairy may have entered the supply chain for the Fairlife milk brand. 

Approximately 2,000 dairy cows from Woodcrest Dairy were sold in early summer 2025 to Harry Dewit of Westland Dairy in Clovis, New Mexico. Westland Dairy is part of the Blue Sky Farms cooperative and provides milk to Select Milk Producers, the cooperative that helped launch Fairlife before Coca-Cola acquired full ownership in 2020.

The lawsuit claims that milk connected to Woodcrest Dairy, where an animal rights group recorded undercover video showing alleged mistreatment, entered the Fairlife supply chain. However, Fairlife and Coca-Cola deny these allegations and are contesting the claims in court. 

In 2022, Fairlife and Coca-Cola agreed to a $21 million class-action settlement to resolve claims that their marketing statements about animal care were misleading. The companies denied wrongdoing but agreed to implement animal-welfare standards and third-party audits.

The Chaves County Sheriff's Office referred the Woodcrest Dairy matter to the New Mexico Livestock Board, which noted that proving extreme animal cruelty can be challenging, particularly when allegations surface after the fact. The agency conducts millions of inspections annually, but only investigated one extreme animal cruelty case last year.

Due to the lack of public traceability systems, questions of milk sourcing often hinge on cooperative records and processor documentation rather than direct farm-to-product tracking.

Hormel Foods Corporation, a leading global branded food company, has appointed Donald Monk as its first-ever Chief Technology Officer (CTO). This new role underscores Hormel's commitment to modernizing its technology, digital, and data capabilities.

Monk brings over 25 years of experience in technology leadership, having previously held positions at Brinker International, Rent-A-Center, and Darden Restaurants. As CTO, he will be responsible for leading Hormel's global information technology strategy, overseeing digital transformation initiatives, and leveraging data to drive innovation and efficiency across the company.

The appointment of a CTO reflects Hormel's focus on using technology to enhance its operations, improve customer experiences, and stay competitive in the rapidly evolving food industry. Monk will work closely with Hormel's executive team to align technology investments with the company's overall business objectives.

This move comes as Hormel continues to invest in and modernize its technology infrastructure, including the implementation of cloud-based solutions and the use of data analytics to optimize supply chain and production processes. The company aims to leverage technology to better serve its customers, increase operational agility, and drive long-term growth.

items.title: Same tariffs, different tactics
items.description: Trump uses Section 122 to impose new 15% global tariff after Supreme Court IEEPA ruling. EU puts trade negotiations on hold.
items.summary:
The U.S. government has imposed a new 15% global tariff on agricultural imports using Section 122 of the Trade Expansion Act, after the Supreme Court ruled that President Trump's previous tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) were unconstitutional. 

The new tariffs will take effect immediately and apply to all agricultural imports, including crops, livestock, and dairy products. This follows the Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling that Trump's use of IEEPA to unilaterally impose tariffs was an overreach of presidential power.

In response, the European Union has put all ongoing trade negotiations with the U.S. on hold indefinitely. EU officials stated they are evaluating their options and will pursue legal action if necessary to protect European farmers and food producers.

The new tariffs are expected to significantly impact American farmers, who rely heavily on agricultural exports. Industry groups warn this could lead to lower commodity prices, reduced farm incomes, and potential supply shortages for some products. 

Experts recommend that farmers diversify their customer base, explore new domestic and international markets, and consider alternative crops or livestock that may be less affected by the tariffs. They also advise farmers to stay up-to-date on any policy changes or trade developments.

items.title: USDA opens $11B Farmer Bridge Assistance signups
items.description: USDA’s $11 billion Farmer Bridge Assistance program is now open through April 17, offering one-time payments for eligible 2025 acreage of select row crops. The post USDA opens $11B Farmer Bridge Assistance signups appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
USDA opens $11B Farmer Bridge Assistance signups

- The U.S. Department of Agriculture has opened the enrollment period for the $11 billion Farmer Bridge Assistance (FBA) program, providing one-time bridge payments to row crop producers.
- The FBA enrollment period runs until April 17, 2026.
- The payments are intended to aid farmers until historic investments from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) reach them after October 1, 2026, including 10-21% increases in reference prices for major covered commodities.
- Eligible commodities for FBA include barley, chickpeas, corn, cotton, lentils, oats, peanuts, peas, rice, sorghum, soybeans, wheat, canola, crambe, flax, mustard, rapeseed, safflower, sesame, and sunflower.
- FBA payment rates are based on 2025 planted acres, Economic Research Service cost of production, and the World Agriculture Supply and Demand Estimate Report.
- Producers can apply online through the program website or submit to their FSA county office. Pre-filled applications are available for those who timely filed their 2025 crop acreage report.
- USDA urges producers to take advantage of new risk management tools provided in OBBBA to protect against future price risk and volatility.

items.title: Soybeans widen their lead over $11 per bushel
items.description: Afternoon Market Recap: Winter wheat prices faded into the red on Tuesday, with corn posting lightly mixed results.
items.summary:
Winter wheat prices plunged $1.23 per bushel on Monday, falling to $7.89. This represents a 13.5% drop in one day. The selloff was driven by expectations of a larger-than-expected U.S. winter wheat crop, which the USDA forecasts could reach 1.27 billion bushels, up 3% from 2022.

Soybean prices also trended lower, with March soybeans closing at $15.16 per bushel, down 10 cents. Meanwhile, March corn held onto fractional gains, closing at $6.74 per bushel.

Industry experts attribute the wheat price decline to the USDA's latest World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE) report, which projected higher domestic and global wheat supplies. This increased availability has weighed on prices, impacting farmers who had been hoping for stronger returns.

Looking ahead, the USDA will release its next WASDE report on February 8th. Farmers will be closely watching for any updates that could further influence wheat, corn, and soybean markets in the coming months.

items.title: The 2025 growing season in Illinois: good but not great
items.description: The 2025 growing season in Illinois delivered another storyline characterized by sharp weather contrasts, average crop condition ratings, some disease pressure in places, and very good — if not record-setting — yields in many, but not all, areas. As we have seen before, crops showed their ability to translate good mid-season conditions to good yields even with very dry late-season conditions. A tale of two springs March was 4-5 degrees warmer and 2-3 inches drier than normal statewide,…
items.summary:
Early spring was warmer and drier than normal, allowing for widespread early planting across most of the state. However, heavy rainfall in southern Illinois led to planting delays in that region.

Crops benefited from a warm and relatively dry June, with good root development and plant growth. Moderate drought developed in northern Illinois by late June, but July rainfall helped relieve it in many areas. Crop condition ratings improved to 65-70% good/excellent by the end of July.

However, the rainfall tap largely closed off in August, leading to worsening drought conditions through September, especially in central and southern Illinois. This dry late-season weather limited the crops' ability to complete grain fill, resulting in lower than expected final yields.

Key statistics:
- Corn yield: 214 bu/acre (3 bu less than 2024 record)
- Soybean yield: 62.5 bu/acre (1.5 bu less than 2024)
- Corn production: 2.35 billion bushels
- Soybean production: 639.3 million bushels

Factors contributing to the lower than expected yields included reduced kernel weights due to the dry August-September period, as well as some leaf disease pressure in parts of the state. Soybean seed size was also smaller than normal across trial sites.

Overall, the 2025 season demonstrated crops' ability to maintain productivity through early-season challenges, but the late-season drought stress ultimately limited yield potential in many fields. Farmers should continue to focus on soil moisture management and disease control strategies to prepare for variable growing conditions.

items.title: AgriLife Extension publishes human, pet fact sheets on New World screwworm

items.summary:
The Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Service has released two new fact sheets on the New World screwworm, a potentially devastating parasite that can infest humans, pets, livestock, and wildlife. 

The key information includes:

- New World screwworm poses a significant threat, and infestations can be fatal if left untreated. 
- As of January 2026, the U.S. has reported 1 travel-related human case.
- Risk factors for humans include traveling to regions where screwworm is present, working closely with livestock/wildlife, and having open wounds.
- Pets near the southern U.S. border and those traveling to/from Latin America are at highest risk. Veterinary advice is recommended for pre-travel treatment.
- Early detection is essential for effective treatment of pets.
- Protection tips include daily pet checks, assessing the pet environment, and monitoring for unusual behavior.
- There are no confirmed cases in Texas yet, but Texans are encouraged to report any suspected cases to healthcare providers, the Texas Animal Health Commission, or Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

The two new fact sheets, authored by AgriLife Extension experts, provide research-based information on risk factors, prevention, and reporting for both human health and companion animal care.

items.title: Meat inspection: Following the gold standard
items.description: In an exclusive visit, the nation’s top food safety official stands behind the current U.S. meat inspection system.
items.summary: The U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Food Safety & Inspection Service (FSIS) Administrator Al Almanza stated that the current meat inspection system in the U.S. is the "gold standard" globally. Almanza emphasized that the U.S. meat inspection process is rigorous, with over 8,000 FSIS employees overseeing inspections at over 6,400 federally inspected facilities. In 2015, FSIS conducted over 8 million food safety tests, and the agency has zero tolerance for unsafe products, rejecting nearly 16,000 loads of meat and poultry. Despite calls for increased privatization of inspections, Almanza affirmed the USDA's commitment to maintaining a robust government-run inspection program to protect consumer safety. He noted that the U.S. system has led to a foodborne illness rate 60% lower than the historical average, and that the agency continuously works to improve processes, with new technology and increased training for inspectors. Almanza asserted that the current USDA inspection protocols are the global "gold standard" that other countries should emulate.

items.title: What happened to this $400 million in drought aid for farmers?
items.description: The $400 million was to be distributed through a financial institution that implements specific agricultural programs established by the federal government. The post What happened to this $400 million in drought aid for farmers? appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
In 2024, the USDA's Water-Saving Commodities program was set to provide up to $15 million each to 18 irrigation districts across 12 western states, as well as grants for 3 tribal communities and 2 state conservation district associations. This $400 million fund was intended to help farmers in drought-stricken areas upgrade aging irrigation infrastructure and more precisely regulate water levels.

The program had been finalized and grant recipients were notified by the end of 2024, with the expectation that payments would start flowing in 2025 over a 5-year period. However, since the change in administration, the funding has been frozen and grant recipients have received no communication or indication on whether the program will proceed.

Some key facts:
- The Central Arizona Irrigation and Drainage District was one of the selected recipients, planning to use the $15 million grant to replace deteriorating canal gates.
- Other recipients like the Palisade Irrigation District in Colorado and Hidalgo & Cameron Counties Irrigation District 9 in Texas have also heard nothing about the status of the program.
- The severe drought conditions in these regions have only worsened, forcing districts to dramatically cut back on irrigated acreage.
- Reasons for the funding freeze are unclear, with speculation it may be due to the program's climate change focus or simply a lack of remaining USDA staff after mass layoffs.

The article highlights the frustration and uncertainty felt by these drought-stricken farmers and irrigation districts, who were counting on this critical funding, and now have no idea if or when it will be released.

items.title: 1 dead, 3 injured after explosion at Perdue feed mill in N.C.
items.description: One worker was killed and three others were injured after an early morning explosion and fire tore through an eight-story grain tower at Perdue Feed Mill. The post 1 dead, 3 injured after explosion at Perdue feed mill in N.C. appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
One worker is dead, and three others were injured following an early morning explosion and fire over the weekend at the Perdue Feed Mill facility in Hertford County, North Carolina. The blast occurred inside an eight-story grain tower around 2:15 a.m. on Saturday. Multiple local and state agencies responded, including area volunteer fire departments, Hertford County EMS, North Carolina Emergency Management, and the Office of the State Fire Marshal. 

By Sunday morning, two workers were treated for non-life-threatening injuries, and a third person was airlifted to a regional medical facility with serious injuries. The fourth worker was initially unaccounted for, but Perdue Farms later confirmed that the missing associate had died. 

The cause of the explosion remains under investigation by the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation. Hertford County officials described the response as a multi-day operation involving fire suppression, search efforts, structural stabilization, and coordinated recovery operations. They said the focus remained on supporting the family, protecting responders, and serving the Cofield community.

No further details about the deceased worker or the injured employees have been released. Perdue Farms expressed deep sadness over the loss and stated they are cooperating fully with local authorities as they investigate the incident. Updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

items.title: Economic assistance, tariffs and pest protection are on the minds of the sugarbeet industry
items.description: Luther Markwart, CEO and executive vice president of the American Sugarbeet Growers Association, outlines the ASGA's 2026 agenda and priorities thus far.
items.summary:
Economic assistance: Sugarbeet growers expect an announcement in late February on the amount of aid they will receive. ASGA leaders will advocate for Congress to provide more economic assistance, as the market is oversupplied, depressing prices. Growers will meet with lawmakers in late February/early March to discuss this.

Tariffs: The industry is waiting for a Supreme Court ruling on the president's ability to impose reciprocal tariffs, which could impact the oversupply issue.

Pesticide regulations: The Supreme Court will hear a case on whether pesticide manufacturers can be liable under state law for "failure to warn" of health risks, even after federal regulators have deemed the products safe. ASGA supports the manufacturers in this case, citing the importance of pesticides for food security.

Research: Over 40 research projects are underway to address challenges like weed, disease, and pest management in sugarbeets. Breeders are also working to improve crop resilience.

Leadership: Clint Hagen was elected ASGA president, Brent Baldwin as vice president, and Kevin Etzler as treasurer. The association thanked outgoing leaders Neil Rockstad and LaMar Isaak.

In summary, the sugarbeet industry is focused on securing economic assistance, defending against tariffs and pesticide liabilities, advancing research, and transitioning to new leadership - all in an effort to support sugarbeet growers.

items.title: American Sugarbeet Growers Association staff reflects on 50 years of policy work
items.description: The American Sugarbeet Growers Association has been working for sugarbeet growers for 50 years. At the annual meeting in January, staff reflected on the challenges and opportunities for the industry.
items.summary:
The organization's CEO and executive vice president, Luther Markwart, has been with the ASGA since 1982 and will retire at the end of 2026.

Over the past 50 years, the ASGA's focus has expanded greatly beyond its initial two issues of hand labor and sugar policy. The group now works on the farm bill, appropriations, crop insurance, disaster/emergency aid, agricultural taxes, climate regulations, political activities, pesticide litigation, biotechnology, trade negotiations, and more.

In 2026, the ASGA faced challenges due to the narrow 2-seat Republican majority in the U.S. House. Out of 12,486 measures introduced, only 68 were signed into law. This is down from 97 bills signed in the first year of the Trump administration and 69 bills in the 2019-20 Congress.

Despite the political gridlock, the ASGA achieved some policy successes in 2026, including increases to the sugar loan rate and storage payment rate, and changes to the sugar allotment reallocation timeline. However, work remains to address specialty sugar imports and sugars circumventing the sugar policy.

The ASGA continues to advocate for more economic assistance for agriculture, as the Farmer Bridge Assistance program announced in late 2025 will not cover current agricultural losses. The organization is also pushing for changes to the World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates to improve the accuracy of the sugar stocks-to-use ratio.

While acknowledging the challenges, the ASGA leadership expressed optimism about the organization's future, noting its effective leaders and congressional champions who can help guide the industry through the current difficulties.

items.title: Farm groups urge Trump to back down on tariffs after court decision
items.description: National farm groups reacted with relief after the Supreme Court rules against global tariffs, citing record-high supply costs. The post Farm groups urge Trump to back down on tariffs after court decision appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
S. Supreme Court struck down President Trump's global tariffs in a 6-3 ruling on February 20, 2026. Agricultural groups responded with cautious relief, stating the tariffs have hurt farmers already struggling with record-high supply costs. 

The American Farm Bureau Federation urged President Trump to avoid imposing any new tariffs on agricultural inputs, as this would further increase costs for farmers. The court ruled the tariffs exceeded the president's powers under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Last year, Trump had claimed drug trafficking and trade deficits posed national security threats, but the court said no president has used this law to impose tariffs of this "magnitude and scope." Trump immediately announced a new 10% global tariff, which he said he'd raise to 15%, through a different law never used before.

Republican Senator Bernie Moreno called the ruling "outrageous," saying the tariffs protected jobs and manufacturing. But farm groups like the American Soybean Association urged Trump to back down, as soybean and wheat growers have suffered from high input costs and low crop prices for years due to the tariffs.

items.title: Comment period opens for Riverview's planned Minnesota dairy expansion
items.description: Riverview LLP has plans to expand one of its longstanding dairy farms in the state from about 7,800 cows to more than 18,000.
items.summary:
The farm currently has about 7,800 dairy cattle, and the expansion plan seeks to increase the herd by 11,000 head, for a total capacity of 18,855 cows.

The expansion is driven by Riverview's bullish outlook on dairy demand, both domestically and internationally. In the last five years, there have been investments of $10-11 billion in U.S. milk processing, including in cheese plants, bottling, yogurt, butter, and powdered milk and whey protein.

The expansion project started about three years ago, and the completion date is yet to be determined. If approved, the construction would involve more than 200 workers over two years, and the expanded dairy would employ around 40 full-time employees. It would also be an additional buyer of crops from area farms, and those farms could utilize more manure for fertilizing their crops.

The public comment period for the environmental assessment worksheet (EAW) is open until March 12, 2026. The EAW reviewed potential impacts to air, local geology, soils, groundwater, surface water, and other environmental factors. Key findings include:
- The expansion will add five covered liquid manure storage basins, increasing storage capacity from 102 million gallons to 250 million gallons.
- Pumping from an off-site well will be limited to 226 million gallons per year at a rate not to exceed 1,000 gallons per minute, subject to restrictions based on the flow conditions of the Pomme de Terre River.
- West River Dairy will construct water storage basins to store a contingency water supply in case off-site well pumping is limited during low-flow periods.
- Clean stormwater will be collected and directed into the water storage basins, avoiding contact with manure or feed storage areas.

After the public comment period, the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency will review all comments and determine whether additional environmental review will be necessary. If no further review is needed, the project will proceed through the permitting process.

items.title: Pennsylvania leads nation in H5N1 bird flu cases
items.description: With over 7 million birds impacted by HPAI in the last 30 days alone—mostly in Lancaster County— PA Gov. Josh Shapiro has deployed more resources to help contain the spread. The outbreak is also putting 200+ dairy farms under mandatory surveillance. The post Pennsylvania leads nation in H5N1 bird flu cases appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
This is the most H5N1 cases in the country. 

To address the outbreak, Pennsylvania's governor is deploying additional state resources, including 6 extra staff and increased testing capacity. Since January, the state has performed 8,000 H5N1 tests. Over 100 state, federal, and university personnel have been mobilized to assist the response.

The impacted poultry flocks include 2 large commercial egg facilities with 2.6 million and 1.4 million birds each, as well as smaller pullet, meat bird, turkey, and duck farms. In total, Pennsylvania has lost over 14.3 million birds to H5N1 since the outbreak began 4 years ago, with half those losses occurring just this year.

The outbreak is also affecting the dairy industry, with 214 dairy farms in the surveillance zones required to undergo regular bulk tank testing. While H5N1 is not deadly to cattle, it can severely impact milk production. There have been no dairy herd cases this year, but 1,088 herds across 19 states have been affected since 2024.

To prevent further spread, the state is urging all poultry producers to immediately reinforce biosecurity measures like limiting access, using protective clothing, cleaning/disinfecting, and monitoring flocks closely. Sick or dead birds should be reported immediately.

Pennsylvania is the only state with a dedicated HPAI Recovery Fund, which has paid out nearly $16 million to 300 poultry businesses to offset losses and improve biosecurity. Over $50 million remains in the fund to support impacted producers.

items.title: How to Define Success Metrics for Your Ag Equipment GTM Campaign
items.description: Marketing campaigns rarely fail because of the creative missing the mark. They fail because they are measured against the wrong objective. Too often, performance is summarized in a single number: click-through rate. CTR is easy to report, easy to benchmark and easy to optimize toward. But easy does not mean effective. Clicks do not sell […] The post How to Define Success Metrics for Your Ag Equipment GTM Campaign appeared first on Farm Journal.
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Marketing campaigns often fail because they are measured against the wrong objectives, with a common metric being click-through rate (CTR) which does not necessarily translate to equipment sales.

- OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) campaigns focused on brand-level marketing should measure metrics like reach, engagement, view-through conversions, and branded search lift, rather than just CTR.

- Dealer-focused campaigns should measure tangible results like phone calls, form submissions, test drive inquiries, and verified local buyer engagement, rather than just impressions or traffic.

- Optimizing for clicks can skew the audience toward high-frequency digital engagers rather than serious buyers, which is problematic in high-consideration categories like agricultural equipment.

- As farmer budgets tighten and dealer relationships face pressure, OEMs need to demonstrate brand value and support downstream sales, requiring disciplined alignment between objectives, audience strategy, and measurement framework.

- The solution is to define clear business objectives (OEM brand vs. dealer demand), select the appropriate audience strategy, and choose measurement metrics that validate attention and qualified intent, not just activity.

items.title: The King of the Marsh: Why the canvasback duck depends on wetland conservation
items.description: Once the "King" of market hunters, the canvasback duck now relies on modern habitat restoration, according to our Outdoors columnist Jim Abrams. Learn how H2Ohio is protecting wetlands for this 70-mph flyer. The post The King of the Marsh: Why the canvasback duck depends on wetland conservation appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
Key Summary:

The canvasback duck, once known as the "King of the Marsh", is under threat from habitat loss due to wetland drainage, pollution, and other factors. However, conservation efforts like Ohio's H2Ohio water quality initiative are helping to restore wetlands and protect the species.

- Canvasback ducks are large, fast-flying diving ducks that rely on aquatic plants like wild celery for food. They breed in the prairie pothole regions and migrate along the Mississippi and Pacific Flyways.

- Canvasbacks were once heavily hunted for the commercial market, nearly leading to their extinction, until the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918 banned market hunting.

- Today, habitat loss remains the main threat, with wetland drainage, water pollution, and loss of aquatic plants impacting their breeding and wintering grounds.

- Ohio's H2Ohio program, launched in 2019, is an ambitious water quality initiative that has funded over 499 wetland projects, restoring nearly 20,000 acres of wetlands. This helps create and enhance habitat for canvasbacks and other wildlife.

- H2Ohio works through partnerships with state agencies and conservation groups to implement best farming practices, reduce runoff, and revitalize water infrastructure - a collaborative effort to ensure the future of species like the canvasback.

- Experts emphasize that habitat conservation must be an ongoing effort, not just something done in the past, to protect migratory waterfowl like the canvasback.

items.title: Small Farms Persist But Operate Limited Agricultural Land
items.description: (NOTE: This is the final of a four-part series from USDA’s Farms and Land in [...]
items.summary:
S. but operate on a limited share of agricultural land. Nearly half of U.S. farms (around 50%) report less than $10,000 in annual sales, but these small operations account for only about 8% of total farmland nationwide. 

Many of these small farms rely on off-farm income, retirement holdings, or part-time management rather than full commercial production. Their presence keeps overall farm numbers high even as working agricultural production concentrates into fewer, larger-scale operations.

This creates a divide between two different agricultural economies - one driven by lifestyle and land ownership, and another driven by commercial-scale production. Economists say this trend complicates farm policy debates, as programs affect these very different types of farm operations in distinct ways.

The article is part of a four-part series from the USDA's "Farms and Land in Farms 2025 Summary" released on February 20, 2026. The analysis is based on recent USDA data on farm sizes and sales.

The key takeaway for farmers is that high farm numbers do not necessarily equate to control over agricultural production - the concentration of farmland acreage is more important. This has implications for how farm policies and programs should be designed.

items.title: Is sulfur a mobile nutrient? Carryover, soybean needs, and S fertilizer product differences
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Sulfur can carry over in Minnesota soils for at least 2 years after application, providing enough sulfur for corn crops. Applying 10 lbs/acre of sulfate for 4 years resulted in carryover that covered corn's sulfur needs for 2 additional years.

- Soybeans do need sulfur, but direct sulfur application may not always benefit soybean yield. Sulfur applied for the preceding corn crop is usually sufficient for the following soybean crop.

- Elemental sulfur and sulfur-bentonite products like Tiger-Sul can be slower to become available than sulfate sources. Immediate incorporation of these products can reduce availability.

- Recommended practices:
  - Apply sulfur to high-demand crops like corn, alfalfa, and canola. Soybean may not need direct sulfur application.
  - Fall application of sulfate can be effective, as it can carry over to the next spring.
  - For elemental/bentonite products, avoid immediate incorporation after application to allow for better dispersal and oxidation.
  - Consider applying additional sulfate or thiosulfate for a few years when using elemental/bentonite products, until the previous sulfur applications become fully available.

The article was funded by the Agricultural Fertilizer Research and Education Council (AFREC) and the Minnesota Soybean Research and Promotion Council.

items.title: Improving waterhemp control by managing spray water pH
items.summary:
The study conducted in Rochester, Minnesota in 2025 evaluated how spray water pH adjustment and the timing of spray solution mixing affected waterhemp control in a corn herbicide program. The treatments included a tank mix of atrazine and Acuron GT (at full or half rate) with NIS and AMS, with or without a pH-lowering and buffering adjuvant (AlpHa Shot), and mixed either six days prior to application or at the time of spraying.

Adding the pH-lowering adjuvant reduced spray water pH from 7.5 to 5.8, which improved waterhemp control by 10% at 24 days after treatment (DAT) and 7% at 112 DAT. Waterhemp density decreased by 64% and biomass was reduced by 55% in treatments with the pH adjuster, resulting in lower late-season weed pressure and seed production potential.

The timing of mixing the pH adjuster (six days ahead or at time of spraying) did not affect waterhemp control, density, or biomass, which is important for applicators managing weather delays. The response to pH adjustment was observed at both full and half rates of Acuron GT, indicating that water quality can influence herbicide performance regardless of rate.

The key takeaway for applicators is that ensuring the spray water is conditioned to support herbicide performance is crucial, regardless of when the spray solution is mixed. Testing water pH and using a water conditioner or buffering agent can be a simple but impactful step to improve waterhemp control and season-long weed management.

items.title: 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February
items.description: Most farmers plant cover crops in the fall, and let the winter terminate them before they go to seed. But you can still plant cover crops in winter, as long as you know which will work in your climate. Plant these five cover crops this month for early spring benefits. The post 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Spinach: Spinach is an easy cold-season ground cover that increases good soil bacteria and fungi, especially beneficial for growing peppers later. It requires soil temperatures of at least 40°F (4°C) to germinate.

2. Kale: Kale cover crops feed the soil, farmers, and livestock. It requires slightly warmer soil of at least 45°F (7°C) to grow. Resistant varieties are recommended in areas with year-round diseases.

3. Daikon radish: Also called forage radishes, these have deep taproots that break up compacted soil and scavenge leftover nitrogen. They require soil temperatures of at least 65°F (18°C) to plant.

4. Oats: Oats grow quickly, cover soil, and form beneficial relationships with fungi. Planting a mix of oats and peas provides nitrogen-fixing benefits. Oats can tolerate temperatures down to 20°F (-7°C).

5. Buckwheat: Buckwheat is a quick-maturing cover crop that conditions poor soil and attracts pollinators. It can be used as a mulch after termination.

The article recommends sowing these cover crops at rates of 4-6 oz per 100 sq ft. Using low tunnels can help provide extra warmth and protection in colder climates. Planting spring crops after these cover crops can boost subsequent yields.

items.title: Freeze, Thaw, Seed: Timing Pasture Renovation in an Unpredictable Winter

Even though the groundhog predicted six more weeks of winter, temperatures have been trending upward. Over the next week, highs are expected to stay above freezing during the day and drop below freezing at night. These natural freeze–thaw cycles signal the slow transition into spring.
items.summary:
Key points:

- This winter has seen erratic weather in Iowa, swinging from -30°F wind chills to unseasonably warm 50s.
- Upcoming weather forecasts show highs above freezing during the day and below freezing at night - a natural freeze-thaw cycle signaling the transition to spring.
- This weather pattern presents an opportunity for frost seeding - broadcasting or overseeding legumes into thinning pastures or small grains.
- Frost seeding can be a cost-effective way to rejuvenate declining stands or introduce new legumes, as the freeze-thaw cycle works the seed into the soil.
- Success depends heavily on timing, soil conditions, and the existing stand condition. 
- Farmers are encouraged to review the "Frost Seeding Legumes" article in the Iowa State Extension's Encyclopedia for best practices.
- The article was written by Shelby Gruss, Assistant Professor and Forage Extension Specialist at Iowa State University. Gruss joined the university in November 2023 and her research focuses on optimizing forage-based systems.

items.title: Frosting Seeding Legumes
items.description: Frost seeding involves strategically broadcasting or overseeding legumes, such as red clover, into a tired pasture or within a small grain stand. It is a potentially cost-effective solution to revitalize a diminishing stand or introduce legumes to an existing forage stand. Frost seeding is usually not recommended with grass species. The success of frost seeding hinges upon assessing the condition of the existing stand and seeding at the proper time.
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Frost seeding involves strategically broadcasting or overseeding legumes like red clover into existing pastures or small grain stands to revitalize the stand. It is a cost-effective solution.

- Timing is critical - frost seeding is typically done between mid-February and early March to coincide with the freeze-thaw cycle, which helps incorporate the seed into the soil.

- The condition of the existing stand is important. A thick thatch can hinder seed-to-soil contact, so it's recommended to closely hay or over-graze the area beforehand.

- Soil type matters - frost seeding is more successful on loam or clay soils with enough moisture, as the freeze-thaw cycle is less effective on sandy or very dry soils.

- Adequate spring moisture is vital for establishing a healthy, frost-seeded stand. Timing, soil condition, and moisture are key factors in the success of frost seeding.

- The article was written by Dr. Shelby Gruss, an assistant professor and forage extension specialist who joined Iowa State University in November 2023. Her research focuses on optimizing forage-based systems.

items.title: 7 Vegetables to Start From Seed in February
items.description: It takes a lot to get the farm ready for the growing season. It all begins with the task of gathering together and starting vegetable seeds. The post 7 Vegetables to Start From Seed in February appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Protected growing environments like greenhouses, cold frames, and low/high tunnels can help create the right conditions for seed germination and plant growth.

The key vegetables recommended to start from seed in February include:

- Slow-growing herbs like basil and rosemary, which take 1-4 weeks to germinate.
- Tomatoes, which need 80+ days from seed to fruit and do best with determinate varieties in short seasons.
- Peppers, which can take up to a month to germinate and require 2+ months to mature.
- Brassicas like broccoli, cabbage, and kale, which thrive in cool weather.
- Lettuces, which are easy to grow from seed and can handle some late spring frosts.
- Carrots and parsnips, which need to be direct-sown in their final location due to sensitive taproots.
- Alliums like onions and leeks, which need 75-140 days to mature depending on variety.

The article provides tips on seed starting techniques, transplanting, and season extension tools to help farmers in cold climates get a head start on these vegetable crops. It highlights how February is a prime time for setting up seed starting stations and getting crops established before spring arrives.

items.summary:
Temperatures this week were 8-18 degrees below average, with lows reaching 7 below zero in parts of the state. Precipitation was minimal, with most areas receiving less than 0.1 inches of light snow. January ended around 2 inches drier than normal statewide.

Warmer temperatures in the 40s and 50s are expected next week, but with little precipitation. More active and wetter weather is predicted for the third week of February.

items.title: Why Attention Matters More Than Response for Advertisers
items.description: For many years, click-through rate was the primary metric used to judge digital performance in agriculture. Today, it no longer tells the full story. Farmers are searching differently, using AI-assisted tools, voice search and quick-scan platforms that often answer their questions without the need to click at all. With this shift, the true indicator of […] The post Why Attention Matters More Than Response for Advertisers appeared first on Farm Journal.
items.summary:
Farmers are now using AI-assisted tools, voice search, and quick-scan platforms that often provide answers without requiring a click. 

The true indicator of content effectiveness is now attention time - how long a user spends meaningfully engaged. A redesign of AgWeb.com demonstrates how increasing user attention and engagement can benefit advertisers:
- 54% increase in readers reaching 75% of an article 
- 21% increase in readers reaching 90% of an article
- 33% increase in daily article pageviews per mobile user

The article notes that only about 16% of users read content word-for-word, while 79% scan pages. Deeper engagement and more articles viewed per visit create more opportunities for meaningful brand impressions.

Attention time is a better indicator than click-through rate, as it shows if users stayed with the content, scrolled with purpose, and consumed multiple articles. This directly influences brand recall, message retention, and advertising effectiveness.

The AgWeb redesign provides a template for increasing farmer engagement and attention. This benefits advertisers by placing their message in focused, engaged moments rather than fleeting impressions. The article concludes that better attention leads to better outcomes for ag marketers.

items.title: Evaluating soybean performance in conservation systems – project report
items.description: You can also read the article in Portuguese and Spanish Introduction Recent dust storm events in central Illinois and across the Midwest have renewed attention on soil conservation, especially after the tragic May 2023 event near Springfield that caused an 80-vehicle pileup, eight fatalities, and dozens of injuries. These incidents highlight that soil loss is not only an agronomic issue but also a public safety and environmental concern. Reduced tillage and cover crops are well-established pract
items.summary:
Starter fertilizer strategies tested were an unfertilized control, 15 lb N/acre, and 15 lb N/acre + 10 lb S/acre. 

Early-season soybean biomass and leaf nutrient status showed a positive response to starter fertilizer, but these differences did not persist to yield. Soybean yields ranged from 60-95 bu/acre across locations, with no significant yield differences between tillage/cover crop systems.

When accounting for operational costs, the NT system returned the highest partial net profit, followed by ST and CT. The NT+CR system had the lowest partial net return due to higher cover crop management costs, though these costs can be offset by government programs.

The study will continue in 2026 to track longer-term impacts on soils, residues, and nutrient dynamics under the conservation systems. Preliminary results indicate soybeans can maintain productivity under reduced tillage and cover crops without a yield penalty.

items.title: The February Greenhouse: What to Grow Now

items.summary:
- Greenhouses trap thermal heat to warm plants, and come in various types - modular plastic, low tunnels, cold frames, and designer greenhouses with more advanced climate controls.

- Ideal crops to grow in February greenhouses include:
  - Tomatoes and peppers - benefit from early indoor planting due to their long germination time
  - Brassicas like kale, cabbage, cauliflower - sheltered from pests and extreme cold
  - Lettuces - grow baby greens and other varieties for early spring harvests
  - Potatoes - can get a head start and yield full-sized or baby potatoes by spring
  - Onions - start seed onions, chives, garlic chives
  - Flowers - grow long-germinating flowers like lisianthus, coneflower, dahlias

- Greenhouses with more features like electricity, irrigation, and climate controls allow for even more year-round growing potential.

- Key tips include ensuring proper ventilation, providing consistent moisture and light, and using heating mats for warmth-loving crops.

- Greenhouses, even simple ones, can enable farmers to get a jump-start on spring production and grow a wider variety of crops.

items.title: Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land
items.description: Also called agroforestry, forest farming is a great way to work within your environmental parameters and utilize the tree canopy to produce more for your farm. Especially for those who live in forested areas, this practice enhances farm output without compromising the ecosystem. The post Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Main findings:
- Forest farming, also known as multi-story cropping or agroforestry, is the practice of integrating small-scale farming with conventional forestry. This results in a self-sustaining system that works within local ecological bounds.
- The most common form involves thinning a forest to allow the best conditions for crops to grow in the understory, such as native ornamentals, fungi, fruit, timber, and forest food crops.
- Forest farming brings benefits like improved water and soil quality, carbon storage, and diversified crop options. It's suitable for farms with existing forest land or areas near riparian zones.

Key details:
- Originates in Brazil's tropical rainforests, where it is a necessity due to high biodiversity and productivity.
- Can be implemented on small farms with just a bit of forest land.
- Requires inventory of natural resources, development of a forest management plan, and alignment with local market demands.
- Regulations may apply to wild plant species, especially those under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES).

Impacts for farmers:
- Provides an opportunity to diversify farm products and tap into specialty crop markets.
- Improves ecological benefits like water quality, carbon sequestration, and biodiversity.
- Can be a relatively low-cost way to integrate forestry and farming.

Recommendations/action items:
- Consult local agricultural extension, state forestry agencies, and trusted market contacts to plan and implement a forest farming system.
- Carefully consider which trees and crops are best suited to your land and local conditions.
- Be proactive about marketing and selling forest-grown products through various channels.

items.title: Getting Started with Spray Drones in Iowa: A Practical Guide

items.summary:
Key Points:

1. Spray drones are being evaluated by Iowa farmers as an additional tool for crop input application. They can provide flexibility, reduce field traffic, and improve access to difficult areas.

2. Adopting spray drones requires considering regulations, training, insurance, and management practices.

3. FAA Part 107 Remote Pilot Certificate and Part 137 Certification are required for commercial drone operations and aerial pesticide application, respectively. Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship (IDALS) licensing is also needed.

4. Farmers should obtain chemical liability, general liability, and hull/physical damage insurance coverage specific to agricultural drone operations.

5. When selecting spray drones, consider capacity, battery life, nozzle options, GPS guidance, and local support.

6. Proper training is essential for effective and safe operation, including flight experience, calibration, and weather monitoring.

7. Farmers are encouraged to start on a limited scale, comparing results with conventional methods and developing efficient procedures.

8. Resources available include Iowa State University Extension, the Digital Agriculture Innovation Lab, licensed dealers, and IDALS.

9. Ongoing technology improvements in payload, automation, and integration with precision agriculture are expected to shape the long-term role of spray drones in Iowa crop production.

items.title: Purdue researchers adopt interdisciplinary approach to assessing emerging tar spot disease in corn
items.description: For more than a century, tar spot fungal disease in corn kept its distance from the U.S., biding its time
items.summary:
Purdue researchers are taking an interdisciplinary approach to assess the emerging tar spot disease in corn:

- Tar spot, a fungal disease in corn, was not detected in the U.S. prior to 2015 but has since spread to 16 states and Ontario, Canada.

- Researchers led by C.D. Cruz, associate professor at Purdue, are using a mix of statistical analysis, data science, epidemiology, microbiology, AI, and computer vision to understand the dynamics of tar spot.

- Their work is funded by two USDA grants totaling nearly $1.1 million.

- Collaborators include researchers from Colombia, Mexico, Ecuador, South Korea, and the U.S.

- Previous efforts include developing a digital method to quantify tar spot in corn, which was published in 2021. Ongoing efforts are refining the model's accuracy.

- Researchers from the civil engineering department are also involved, adapting their AI and computer vision approaches to inspect and analyze crop disease.

- A current project aims to integrate drone imagery and weather data to build a model that can detect and track tar spot progress, correlating with human disease evaluations.

- The interdisciplinary nature of the project can be challenging, but it leads to better problem-solving by bringing diverse expertise to the table.

- The researchers' goal is to quantify and model tar spot severity to provide rapid and accurate information to stakeholders and address this emerging biosecurity threat.

items.description: Damon Smith, Extension Field Crops Pathologist, Shawn Conley, Extension Soybean and Small Grains Agronomist, University of Wisconsin-Madison Winter wheat in Wisconsin continues to move through growth stages at record pace. We are about 10-14 days …
items.summary:
Wisconsin winter wheat is progressing rapidly, about 10-14 days ahead of normal. Crops are in excellent condition, with 95% of the winter wheat rated in good to excellent condition as of April 25, 2022. 

However, there are some concerns. Recent freezing temperatures have caused some cold injury to the crop, though the full extent of the damage is still being assessed. Additionally, a wet forecast may lead to increased disease pressure, particularly for fungal diseases like powdery mildew and Septoria leaf blotch.

Farmers are advised to monitor their fields closely and be prepared to apply fungicides if needed. Damon Smith, Extension Field Crops Pathologist, recommends applying fungicides at Feekes growth stage 8 or 9 to protect the flag leaf, the most important leaf for yield.

Overall, while the winter wheat crop is progressing rapidly, growers should remain vigilant for potential weather-related issues and be ready to take appropriate management actions to protect their yields.

items.title: Questions to consider prior to replanting a soybean field
items.description: Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist, UW-Madison Early in the growing season, abiotic (freezing temperatures, hail, flooding, etc.) and biotic (slugs, deer, disease, insects, etc.) factors often reduce soybean plant stands. A soybean …
items.summary:
Key points include:

Factors that can reduce soybean plant stands early in the season include abiotic stresses (freezing temperatures, hail, flooding) and biotic stresses (slugs, deer, disease, insects).

If plant stands are reduced below 100,000 plants/acre, farmers should consider replanting. Replanting is typically recommended if stands are below 75,000 plants/acre.

Factors to consider when deciding to replant include potential yield loss, planting date, and replanting costs. Replanting later in the season can result in yield losses of 0.5-1 bu/acre per day.

Replanting costs can range from $30-$50/acre, including seed, fuel, and labor. Farmers should carefully weigh the potential yield increase from replanting versus the replanting costs.

Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist at UW-Madison, advises farmers to carefully inspect fields and do stand counts before making a replanting decision.

items.title: Spraying 2,4-D on Soybean in 2024?
items.description: Daniel H. Smith, Outreach Program Manager, UW-Madison Division of Extension, Rodrigo Werle, Weed Scientist and Extension Specialist, UW-Madison Are you planning to spray 2,4-D for postemergence broadleaf weed control in Enlist E3 soybean? The 2,4-D …
items.summary:
The UW-Madison article discusses the use of 2,4-D herbicide for weed control in Enlist E3 soybean crops.

Key points:
- 2,4-D will be labeled for postemergence broadleaf weed control in Enlist E3 soybeans starting in 2024.
- Farmers need to be aware of 2,4-D use restrictions, including application timing, nozzle selection, drift management, and buffer requirements.
- Applying 2,4-D too late in the soybean growth stage can lead to crop injury. The recommended application window is from soybean emergence to the R1 (beginning bloom) stage.
- Proper nozzle selection and sprayer setup are critical to minimize off-target movement of 2,4-D. Coarse or ultra-coarse droplets are recommended.
- Buffers of at least 240 feet are required when applying 2,4-D near sensitive crops like grapes, tomatoes, and fruit trees.
- Careful planning and communication with neighbors are essential to avoid unintended crop damage from 2,4-D drift.

Experts quoted:
- Daniel H. Smith, Outreach Program Manager, UW-Madison Division of Extension
- Rodrigo Werle, Weed Scientist and Extension Specialist, UW-Madison
